{
  "research_question": "How does the stimulation paradigm (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, Sham) affect mouse navigation performance metrics including Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion (AD)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "The Combined paradigm yielded the highest success rate (0.7798) and the lowest mean Time-to-Target (2.56 seconds) among all groups.",
    "The Sham group demonstrated the poorest performance across all metrics, with the lowest success rate (0.2733), the highest Time-to-Target (4.68 seconds), and the lowest Path Efficiency (0.3084).",
    "Visual-only paradigms (Dim and Bright) showed intermediate success rates (0.6733 and 0.7845 respectively) but had higher Time-to-Target values compared to the Combined group.",
    "ICMS Only stimulation resulted in a success rate (0.6854) and Time-to-Target (3.05 seconds) similar to Dim Visual Only, but with slightly lower Path Efficiency.",
    "Angular Dispersion (AD) was highest in the Combined group (0.3994) and lowest in the Sham group (0.2360), suggesting different navigational strategies or stability across conditions.",
    "Average Speed was generally consistent across paradigms, ranging from 10.74 (Sham) to 12.83 (Combined) units, with no extreme outliers."
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "The most dramatic difference is in the Success metric, where the Sham group (0.2733) performed significantly worse than all other paradigms, which ranged from 0.67 to 0.78.",
    "Time-to-Target shows the largest gap between the Sham group (4.68s) and the Combined group (2.56s), indicating a substantial delay in target acquisition without combined stimulation.",
    "Path Efficiency is markedly lower in the Sham group (0.3084) compared to the visual and combined groups (0.43-0.50), suggesting less direct paths to the target in the Sham condition.",
    "AD (Angular Dispersion) varies notably, with the Combined group showing the highest dispersion (0.3994) and the Sham group the lowest (0.2360), implying that combined stimulation may lead to more variable turning angles despite better overall success."
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "Combined stimulation appears to be the most effective paradigm for facilitating successful and efficient mouse navigation, reducing time to target and improving path efficiency compared to single-modality stimulations or sham controls. The Sham group's poor performance suggests that the baseline behavior without stimulation is insufficient for the task. While ICMS and visual-only stimulations offer some benefit over Sham, they do not match the efficacy of the Combined approach. The higher AD in the Combined group might indicate a trade-off where increased success comes with less consistent angular trajectories, or it may reflect a more exploratory yet ultimately successful strategy.",
  "limitations": [
    "The analysis relies solely on summary statistics (mean, SD, n) from the provided artifacts; individual subject-level data is not available to assess variance within groups or perform statistical significance testing.",
    "The 'AD' metric is interpreted as angular dispersion based on the prompt, but the specific definition of this variable in the original dataset is not explicitly detailed beyond the column name.",
    "The sample sizes vary significantly between paradigms (Sham n=3505 vs Combined n=48846), which could influence the robustness of the mean estimates for smaller groups.",
    "No information is provided regarding the specific parameters of the stimulation (e.g., intensity, duration) or the exact nature of the 'Combined' stimulation protocol."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Conduct an ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test on each response variable to determine if the observed differences in means are statistically significant, followed by post-hoc pairwise comparisons (e.g., Tukey's HSD) to identify specific differences between paradigms.
